learn.hook: Toss a coin 10 times and you might get 7 heads. Toss it 10,000 times and something magical happens — it settles near half!
points: Experimental (empirical) probability comes from actually doing trials: P(E) = (number of trials in which E happened) ÷ (total number of trials).
Theoretical probability comes from reasoning about equally likely outcomes. As the number of trials grows, the experimental value gets closer to the theoretical one.
An event is a collection of outcomes of an experiment, e.g. 'getting an even number' on a die = {2, 4, 6}.
An elementary event has exactly ONE outcome, e.g. 'getting a 5'. The probabilities of all the elementary events of an experiment add up to 1.

example.q: A coin is tossed 200 times and shows heads 108 times. Find the experimental and theoretical probabilities of a head.
steps: Theoretical: two equally likely outcomes, H and T
They are close, and would get closer with more tosses

quiz.q: A coin is tossed 200 times and lands heads 108 times. What is the experimental probability of a head?
quiz.explain: Experimental P(H) = 108/200 = 0.54.
steps: Experimental probability = (number of heads) ÷ (number of tosses).
quiz.mistake: Gives the theoretical value 0.5 instead

quiz.q: For a fair coin, what is the theoretical probability of a head?
quiz.explain: There are two equally likely outcomes, H and T, and one is favourable: P(H) = 1/2.
steps: A fair coin has 2 equally likely outcomes, H and T; 1 is favourable.
quiz.mistake: Uses results from an experiment instead

quiz.q: A die is rolled. How many outcomes are in the event 'a number greater than 4'?
quiz.explain: The event is {5, 6}, which has 2 outcomes.
steps: A die shows 1–6; numbers greater than 4 are 5 and 6.
quiz.mistake: Includes 4 itself

quiz.q: What are the elementary events when one coin is tossed, and what do their probabilities add up to?
options: H and T; they add up to 1
HH, HT, TT; they add up to 1
H and T; they add up to 1/2
quiz.explain: Each toss has two single outcomes, H and T, each with probability 1/2, and 1/2 + 1/2 = 1.
steps: One toss has two single outcomes: H and T (the elementary events).
Answer: H and T; they add up to 1
quiz.mistake: Forgets that all elementary events together must add up to 1

quiz.q: A die has six elementary events. What is the sum of their probabilities?
quiz.explain: Each has probability 1/6, and 6 × 1/6 = 1.
steps: Each face of a fair die has probability 1/6.
quiz.mistake: Adds the face numbers or gives one probability

quiz.q: A spinner can stop on A, B or C only. P(A) = 0.5 and P(B) = 0.3. What is P(C)?
quiz.explain: The probabilities of all the elementary events add up to 1, so P(C) = 1 − 0.5 − 0.3 = 0.2.
steps: The probabilities of all elementary events add up to 1.
quiz.mistake: Adds the given probabilities instead of subtracting from 1

quiz.q: Ravi tosses a coin 10 times and gets 7 heads. Neha tosses one 10,000 times. Whose experimental probability of a head is likely to be closer to 1/2?
options: Ravi's, because 7 is a whole number
Neha's, because with more trials the experimental value gets closer to the theoretical one
Neither can ever be close to 1/2
quiz.explain: Over a large number of trials, the experimental probability settles near the theoretical probability.
steps: As the number of trials grows, the experimental probability settles near the theoretical value 1/2.
Neha's 10,000 tosses are far more than Ravi's 10, so hers is likely closer.
Answer: Neha's, because with more trials the experimental value gets closer to the theoretical one
quiz.mistake: Thinks a small number of trials is just as reliable

quiz.q: A die is rolled. Which of these is NOT an elementary event?
quiz.explain: 'Getting an odd number' has three outcomes (1, 3, 5), so it is not elementary.
steps: An elementary event has exactly one outcome.
'Getting an odd number' = {1, 3, 5} has three outcomes, so it is not elementary.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any event described in a few words is elementary

steps: 0.7, 2/3 ≈ 0.67 and 15% = 0.15 are allowed; −0.2 is negative, so it is impossible.

quiz.q: Riya says: 'Either it will rain tomorrow or it won't, so P(rain) = 1/2.' What is wrong with her reasoning?
options: The two outcomes are not equally likely
quiz.explain: P = favourable/total only works when outcomes are equally likely. Rain and no rain usually are not.
steps: P = favourable ÷ total works only when outcomes are equally likely.
'Rain' and 'no rain' are usually not equally likely, so P(rain) = 1/2 is wrong.
Answer: The two outcomes are not equally likely
quiz.mistake: Uses the formula without checking that outcomes are equally likely

On a fair die P(1) = P(6) = 1/6 ✓. The others differ (e.g. girl 30/40 vs boy 10/40).

quiz.q: Two coins are tossed together. What is the probability of getting exactly one head?
quiz.explain: Outcomes: HH, HT, TH, TT. Exactly one head: HT and TH, so P = 2/4 = 1/2.
steps: Outcomes for two coins: HH, HT, TH, TT (4).

quiz.q: A die is rolled. What is the probability of NOT getting a multiple of 3?
quiz.explain: Multiples of 3 are 3 and 6, so P(multiple of 3) = 2/6 = 1/3. P(not) = 1 − 1/3 = 2/3.
steps: Multiples of 3 on a die: 3, 6 → P = 2/6 = 1/3.

quiz.q: Three coins are tossed. What is the probability of getting at least two heads?
quiz.explain: Outcomes with at least 2 heads: HHH, HHT, HTH, THH — 4 of the 8 outcomes. P = 4/8 = 1/2.

steps: Outcomes: HH, HT, TH, TT (4). Match: HH, TT → 2; different: HT, TH → 2.
P(Harpreet) = 2/4 = 1/2 = P(Arjun), so the game is fair.

quiz.explain: Perfect squares up to 50: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49 — that is 7. P = 7/50.

quiz.q: A card is drawn from a deck of 52. What is the probability that it is a black card but not a king?
quiz.explain: There are 26 black cards, including 2 black kings. 26 − 2 = 24, so P = 24/52 = 6/13.

quiz.q: Meena's bag has 5 blue balls and P(blue) = 1/4. How many balls are in the bag?
quiz.explain: 5/total = 1/4, so total = 5 × 4 = 20.

quiz.q: A bag has 5 red balls and some blue balls. P(blue) is twice P(red). How many blue balls are there?

steps: P(blue) = blue/total and P(red) = red/total share the same total.
quiz.mistake: Doubles the total instead of the number of red balls

topics.title: Equally likely? Birthdays, tricky statements and recap

learn.hook: A leap year has an extra day — so the chance of 53 Sundays isn't what you'd guess. Let's think carefully!
points: P(E) = favourable ÷ total works ONLY when the outcomes are equally likely. Win/lose/tie in a cricket match, or pass/fail in an exam, are NOT equally likely.

A leap year has 366 days = 52 weeks + 2 extra days. The 2 extra days can be any of 7 equally likely pairs (Mon–Tue, Tue–Wed, …), and 2 of these contain a Sunday, so P(53 Sundays) = 2/7. An ordinary year has 1 extra day, giving 1/7.
Birthdays: if P(two students have different birthdays) is known, then P(same birthday) = 1 − that value.
Recap: 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1; P(impossible) = 0; P(sure) = 1; P(E) + P(not E) = 1. A probability can never be negative or more than 1.

example.q: What is the probability that a leap year has 53 Sundays?
steps: The two extra days are one of 7 equally likely pairs: (Mon, Tue), (Tue, Wed), …, (Sun, Mon)
Pairs containing Sunday: (Sat, Sun) and (Sun, Mon) — 2 of them

Passing and failing are not equally likely; it depends on preparation.
For a fair coin, head and tail are equally likely.
Neither side is favoured.
Experimental probability is found by reasoning, without doing any trials.
That is theoretical probability.
P(not E) = 1 − P(E).
E and not E together are certain.

Win, loss and tie are not equally likely (a tie is rare), so P(win) = 1/3 is wrong.
